content: The studies reviewed provide detailed insights into the associations between physical activity (PA) and various health-related outcomes, particularly in children and adolescents. 1. Associations Between Physical Activity and Aerobic Fitness: Positive associations between total physical activity (PA) and aerobic fitness were observed in the overall sample (Eiberg et al., 2005; Andersen et al., 2006; Ruiz et al., 2006; Rizzo et al., 2007; Ruiz et al., 2011; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2012). These associations were significant in boys but not in girls (Dencker et al., 2010; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013c). Positive associations were also found in 9-year-olds but not in 15-year-olds (Kristensen et al., 2010). 2. Vigorous Physical Activity (VPA) and Aerobic Fitness: Dencker et al. (2010) reported a positive association between vigorous physical activity (VPA) and aerobic fitness in boys, but not in girls. 3. Moderate-to-Vigorous Physical Activity (MVPA) and Aerobic Fitness: Positive associations between MVPA and aerobic fitness were observed in the total sample (Eiberg et al., 2005; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2010a; Ruiz et al., 2011; Ottevaere et al., 2011; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2012). Subgroup analyses showed positive associations in boys but not in girls (Dencker et al., 2010; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013b). 4. Moderate Physical Activity (MPA) and Aerobic Fitness: From the HELENA cohort, Martinez-Gomez et al. (2010a) and Ottevaere et al. (2011) reported positive associations between moderate physical activity (MPA) and aerobic fitness in the total sample. Martinez-Gomez et al. (2012) found no association, while Jimenez-Pavon et al. (2013c) reported a positive association in boys but not in girls. 5. Physical Activity and Muscular Fitness: Total PA was positively associated with standing broad jump performance in boys but showed no association with upper body or other lower body strength and endurance measures. No associations were observed with any muscular fitness outcomes in girls (Moliner-Urdiales et al., 2010). Hands et al. (2009) found no correlation between total PA and abdominal muscle endurance (curl-ups) or upper body strength, but higher tertiles of total PA were associated with better grip strength. 6. MVPA and Muscular Fitness: MVPA was positively associated with lower body strength but not upper body strength in one study (Aggio et al., 2015). No associations were found between MVPA and upper or lower body strength in boys and girls, except for a positive association with standing broad jump in boys (Moliner-Urdiales et al., 2010). 7. Cardiometabolic Health and Physical Activity: Moderate evidence suggests that physical activity is positively associated with cardiometabolic health in children and adolescents, particularly for plasma triglycerides (TG) and insulin levels. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) was associated with improvements in systolic and diastolic blood pressure (BP), although only a few randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reported statistically significant differences compared to moderate-intensity training or control groups (Eddolls et al., 2017). Resistance training showed limited evidence of statistically significant positive effects on cardiometabolic health outcomes (Bea et al., 2017). 8. Blood Pressure and Physical Activity: Meeting physical activity guidelines was associated with reduced odds of high blood pressure (BP) in one study (de Moraes et al., 2015). Total PA showed favorable dose-response gradients for hypertension (Mark and Janssen, 2008) and diastolic BP (Knowles et al., 2013), but associations with systolic BP were mixed or null across studies. 9. Blood Lipids and Physical Activity: Total PA was favorably associated with HDL cholesterol in one study (Hjorth et al., 2014a). Associations with triglycerides (TG) were mixed, with some studies reporting favorable or null associations (Andersen et al., 2006; Ekelund et al., 2006; Chaput et al., 2013). 10. Insulin Sensitivity and Resistance: Associations between PA and insulin sensitivity/resistance were mixed. Some studies reported favorable associations in boys but not in girls (Telford et al., 2009), while others found null associations (Hjorth et al., 2014a). 11. Liver Fat and Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT): A favorable association was observed between physical activity and liver fat/GGT levels in one study (Anderson et al., 2016). 12. Quality of Evidence: The quality of evidence from cross-sectional studies was rated as low due to limitations in study design and variability in reported outcomes. Moderate evidence supports the positive association between physical activity and cardiometabolic health, particularly for plasma triglycerides and insulin. In summary, physical activity, particularly moderate-to-vigorous and vigorous intensities, is associated with improved aerobic fitness, muscular fitness, and cardiometabolic health in children and adolescents. However, the strength and consistency of these associations vary by sex, age, and specific health outcomes.
